claim: Many viruses have pressurized genomes inside their viral protein shell (capsid).
source: Many viruses previously have been shown to have pressurized genomes inside their viral protein shell, termed the capsid.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on bacteriophages, archaeoviruses, and eukaryotic viruses

claim: Capsid pressure results from tight confinement of negatively charged viral nucleic acids inside the capsid.
source: This pressure results from the tight confinement of negatively charged viral nucleic acids inside the capsid.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models and prior measurements

claim: Internal DNA pressure of tens of atmospheres inside a herpesvirus capsid powers ejection of the viral genome into a host cell nucleus.
source: In this work, we show that the internal DNA pressure of tens of atmospheres inside a herpesvirus capsid powers ejection of the viral genome into a host cell nucleus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from osmotic suppression and pull-down assays presented in the manuscript

claim: This is the first demonstration of a pressure-dependent mechanism of viral genome penetration into a host nucleus leading to infection of eukaryotic cells.
source: To our knowledge, this provides the first demonstration of a pressure-dependent mechanism of viral genome penetration into a host nucleus, leading to infection of eukaryotic cells.
evidence: Based on the novelty of the experimental findings presented in this work

claim: Bacteriophages have pressurized genomes exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure inside their capsids.
source: Recent studies have found that many families of viruses have highly stressed packaged genomes, exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure, inside their viral protein shell, termed the capsid [e.g. bacteriophages (Evilevitch et al., 2003), archaeoviruses (Hanhijärvi et al., 2013) and eukaryotic viruses (Bauer et al., 2013), infecting all three domains of life].
evidence: Supported by citation to Evilevitch et al., 2003

claim: Archaeoviruses have pressurized genomes exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure inside their capsids.
source: Recent studies have found that many families of viruses have highly stressed packaged genomes, exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure, inside their viral protein shell, termed the capsid [e.g. bacteriophages (Evilevitch et al., 2003), archaeoviruses (Hanhijärvi et al., 2013) and eukaryotic viruses (Bauer et al., 2013), infecting all three domains of life].
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanhijärvi et al., 2013

claim: Eukaryotic viruses have pressurized genomes exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure inside their capsids.
source: Recent studies have found that many families of viruses have highly stressed packaged genomes, exerting tens of atmospheres of pressure, inside their viral protein shell, termed the capsid [e.g. bacteriophages (Evilevitch et al., 2003), archaeoviruses (Hanhijärvi et al., 2013) and eukaryotic viruses (Bauer et al., 2013), infecting all three domains of life].
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2013

claim: The pressure in viral capsids results from tight confinement of negatively charged double-stranded viral DNA or dsRNA inside the capsid.
source: The pressure results from tight confinement of the negatively charged double-stranded (ds) viral DNA or dsRNA inside the capsid (Tzlil et al., 2003; Kindt et al., 2001; Purohit et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: HSV-1 capsid contains DNA pressure of 20 atmospheres.
source: Our recent measurement of 20 atmospheres of DNA pressure in a Herpes simplex type 1 (HSV-1) capsid (Bauer et al., 2013) was the first demonstration of a pressurized genome state in a eukaryotic virus.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior measurement by Bauer et al., 2013

claim: The measurement of 20 atmospheres of DNA pressure in HSV-1 capsid was the first demonstration of a pressurized genome state in a eukaryotic virus.
source: Our recent measurement of 20 atmospheres of DNA pressure in a Herpes simplex type 1 (HSV-1) capsid (Bauer et al., 2013) was the first demonstration of a pressurized genome state in a eukaryotic virus.
evidence: Based on the novelty claim and citation to Bauer et al., 2013

claim: High internal capsid pressure is generated by an ATP-driven packaging motor located at a unique capsid vertex.
source: This high internal capsid pressure is generated by an ATP-driven packaging motor located at a unique capsid vertex, shown to be the strongest molecular motor known (McElwee et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to McElwee et al., 2018 and Smith et al., 2001

claim: The ATP-driven packaging motor is the strongest molecular motor known.
source: This high internal capsid pressure is generated by an ATP-driven packaging motor located at a unique capsid vertex, shown to be the strongest molecular motor known (McElwee et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to McElwee et al., 2018 and Smith et al., 2001

claim: Structural features of packaging motor components are shared by bacterial and archaeal dsDNA viruses and eukaryotic herpesviruses.
source: Structural features of packaging motor components are shared by bacterial and archaeal dsDNA viruses and eukaryotic herpesviruses (Krupovic and Bamford, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krupovic and Bamford, 2011

claim: Pressure-driven genome release is one of the central mechanisms of viral replication.
source: This strongly suggests that once DNA is packaged with high force into a capsid, the reverse process of pressure-driven genome release is one of the central mechanisms of viral replication.
evidence: Inferred from the shared structural features of packaging motors across viral domains

claim: A previous attempt to demonstrate pressure-driven ejection mechanism analyzed the velocity of DNA ejection from phage λ into an E. coli cell.
source: A previous attempt to demonstrate this mechanism analyzed the velocity of DNA ejection from phage λ into an E. coli cell to determine whether ejection dynamics correlates with a decrease in intracapsid DNA pressure (Van Valen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Valen et al., 2012

claim: Large cell-to-cell variability in ejection rates made the results of phage λ ejection velocity analysis difficult to interpret.
source: However, due to large cell-to-cell variability in the ejection rates, the results were difficult to interpret.
evidence: Based on assessment of prior work by Van Valen et al., 2012

claim: Phage λ ejection dynamics show timescale variability ranging from a few seconds to minutes.
source: We recently found, using isothermal titration calorimetry, similar timescale variability in phage λ ejection dynamics, ranging from a few seconds to minutes; this variability is caused by the metastable state of the tightly packaged genome resulting from DNA-DNA electrostatic sliding friction, which can delay or stall the ejection process despite high pressure in the capsid.
evidence: Based on recent findings using isothermal titration calorimetry

claim: Variability in phage λ ejection dynamics is caused by the metastable state of the tightly packaged genome resulting from DNA-DNA electrostatic sliding friction.
source: We recently found, using isothermal titration calorimetry, similar timescale variability in phage λ ejection dynamics, ranging from a few seconds to minutes; this variability is caused by the metastable state of the tightly packaged genome resulting from DNA-DNA electrostatic sliding friction, which can delay or stall the ejection process despite high pressure in the capsid.
evidence: Based on recent findings using isothermal titration calorimetry

claim: DNA-DNA electrostatic sliding friction can delay or stall the ejection process despite high pressure in the capsid.
source: We recently found, using isothermal titration calorimetry, similar timescale variability in phage λ ejection dynamics, ranging from a few seconds to minutes; this variability is caused by the metastable state of the tightly packaged genome resulting from DNA-DNA electrostatic sliding friction, which can delay or stall the ejection process despite high pressure in the capsid.
evidence: Based on recent findings using isothermal titration calorimetry

claim: Interstrand friction in phage λ was significantly reduced by a transition in intracapsid DNA structure induced by optimum environmental conditions favorable for infection.
source: However, this interstrand friction was significantly reduced by a transition in intracapsid DNA structure induced by optimum environmental conditions favorable for infection, leading to essentially instant DNA release (Evilevitch, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evilevitch, 2018

claim: Optimum environmental conditions favorable for infection lead to essentially instant DNA release from phage λ.
source: However, this interstrand friction was significantly reduced by a transition in intracapsid DNA structure induced by optimum environmental conditions favorable for infection, leading to essentially instant DNA release (Evilevitch, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evilevitch, 2018

claim: The role that high DNA pressure in phage capsids might play in viral genome delivery into a bacterial cell remained unclear.
source: Thus, the role that high DNA pressure in phage capsids might play in viral genome delivery into a bacterial cell remained unclear.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Experimental evidence placing the discovery of intracapsid genome pressure in the context of eukaryotic viral infection was lacking.
source: Furthermore, the experimental evidence placing the discovery of intracapsid genome pressure (Bauer et al., 2013) in the context of eukaryotic viral infection was lacking.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: DNA pressure in HSV-1 capsids powers ejection of the viral genome into a cell nucleus.
source: Here, we conducted a stringent test, showing that DNA pressure in HSV-1 capsids powers ejection of the viral genome into a cell nucleus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from osmotic suppression and pull-down assays

claim: Herpesviridae are a leading cause of human viral disease, second only to influenza and cold viruses.
source: Herpesviridae are a leading cause of human viral disease, second only to influenza and cold viruses (Pellett and Roizmann, 2007; Roizmann et al., 2007; Sandri-Goldin, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pellett and Roizmann, 2007; Roizmann et al., 2007; Sandri-Goldin, 2006

claim: Nine herpesviruses are human pathogens.
source: The herpesviridae family includes a diverse set of viruses, nine of which are human pathogens (Davison et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davison et al., 2009

claim: Herpesvirus infections are life-long with latency periods between recurrent reactivations.
source: Herpesvirus infections are life-long with latency periods between recurrent reactivations, making treatment difficult (Davison et al., 2009; Pai and Weinberger, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davison et al., 2009; Pai and Weinberger, 2017

claim: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions.
source: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions, encephalitis (Roizmann et al., 2007), shingles (Coen, 2006), birth defects and transplant failures, as well as oncogenic transformation (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roizmann et al., 2007

claim: Herpesvirus infections can cause encephalitis.
source: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions, encephalitis (Roizmann et al., 2007), shingles (Coen, 2006), birth defects and transplant failures, as well as oncogenic transformation (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roizmann et al., 2007

claim: Herpesvirus infections can cause shingles.
source: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions, encephalitis (Roizmann et al., 2007), shingles (Coen, 2006), birth defects and transplant failures, as well as oncogenic transformation (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coen, 2006

claim: Herpesvirus infections can cause birth defects and transplant failures.
source: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions, encephalitis (Roizmann et al., 2007), shingles (Coen, 2006), birth defects and transplant failures, as well as oncogenic transformation (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007

claim: Herpesvirus infections can cause oncogenic transformation.
source: Herpesvirus infections frequently reactivate to result in recurrent acute oral and genital lesions, encephalitis (Roizmann et al., 2007), shingles (Coen, 2006), birth defects and transplant failures, as well as oncogenic transformation (Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rickinson and Kieff, 2007; Ganem, 2007

claim: Herpesviruses consist of a double-stranded DNA genome packaged within an icosahedral capsid that is surrounded by an unstructured protein layer (the tegument) and a lipid envelope.
source: Herpesviruses consist of a double-stranded (ds) DNA genome packaged within an icosahedral capsid that is surrounded by an unstructured protein layer, the tegument, and a lipid envelope.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of herpesvirus structure

claim: After binding at the outer membrane, HSV-1 viruses enter the cell cytoplasm and are transported toward the nucleus.
source: After binding at the outer membrane (Figure 1a), viruses enter the cell cytoplasm and are transported toward the nucleus (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 1

claim: The viral capsid ejects its genome upon docking to a nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: The viral capsid ejects its genome upon docking to a nuclear pore complex (NPC), which forms a passageway for molecular traffic into the nucleus (Figure 1c)(Sodeik et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 1c and citation to Sodeik et al., 1997

claim: Nuclear pore complex (NPC) forms a passageway for molecular traffic into the nucleus.
source: The viral capsid ejects its genome upon docking to a nuclear pore complex (NPC), which forms a passageway for molecular traffic into the nucleus (Figure 1c)(Sodeik et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NPC function and citation to Sodeik et al., 1997

claim: DNA ejection from isolated HSV-1 capsids into solution can be suppressed by creating an osmotic pressure in the host solution that matches the pressure of the packaged DNA.
source: We had shown previously that DNA ejection from isolated HSV-1 capsids into solution can be suppressed by creating an osmotic pressure in the host solution, which matches the pressure of the packaged DNA (Bauer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2013

claim: Osmotic pressure that matches the pressure of packaged DNA effectively eliminates genome pressure in the capsid.
source: This effectively eliminates genome pressure in the capsid (the mechanism of osmotic suppression is explained below).
evidence: Based on the mechanism of osmotic suppression explained in the manuscript

claim: Viral genome ejection through the NPCs into a cell nucleus can be completely suppressed in the presence of the biologically inert osmolyte polyethylene glycol (PEG).
source: In this work we show that viral genome ejection through the NPCs into a cell nucleus can be completely suppressed in the presence of the biologically inert osmolyte polyethylene glycol (PEG).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from osmotic suppression assays

claim: The reconstituted nuclei system accurately reproduces capsids-nuclei binding and nuclear transport of the herpes genome into living cells.
source: The reconstituted nuclei system accurately reproduces capsids-nuclei binding and nuclear transport of the herpes genome into living cells (Ojala et al., 2000; Adam et al., 1990; Au et al., 2016; Cassany and Gerace, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Adam et al., 1990; Au et al., 2016; Cassany and Gerace, 2008

claim: The reconstituted nuclei system provides the benefit of isolating the effect of eliminated capsid pressure on the single step of viral DNA ejection.
source: It provides the benefit of isolating the effect of eliminated capsid pressure on the single step of viral DNA ejection, while avoiding interference from hyperosmotic conditions on other processes occurring within the cell during viral replication.
evidence: Based on the experimental design rationale

claim: All herpesviruses have strongly confined dsDNA inside the capsid, which is released into a cell nucleus upon the capsid docking to the NPCs at the nuclear envelope.
source: All herpesviruses have strongly confined dsDNA inside the capsid, which is released into a cell nucleus upon the capsid docking to the NPCs at the nuclear envelope (Heming et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heming et al., 2017

claim: HSV-1 is a prototypical, experimental model system to study herpesvirus replication due to the ease of growing and purifying large quantities of viral C-capsids.
source: We used HSV-1, which is a prototypical, experimental model system to study herpesvirus replication due to the ease of growing and purifying large quantities of viral C-capsids (DNA-filled capsids without a lipid envelope and tegument proteins)(Méndez-Álvarez, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Méndez-Álvarez, 2000

claim: Viral capsids are permeable to water and small ions.
source: Viral capsids are permeable to water and small ions (Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003

claim: In an aqueous buffer solution without osmolyte addition, water is drawn into the capsid due to the high DNA concentration inside the capsid.
source: In an aqueous buffer solution (without osmolyte addition), due to the high DNA concentration inside the capsid, water is drawn into the ﬁxed volume through the capsid pores, as a result of the entropic drive to maximize mixing, and a large osmotic pressure is developed inside the capsid to equalize the chemical potential of water inside and outside of the capsid.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic pressure

claim: Large osmotic pressure is developed inside the capsid to equalize the chemical potential of water inside and outside of the capsid.
source: In an aqueous buffer solution (without osmolyte addition), due to the high DNA concentration inside the capsid, water is drawn into the ﬁxed volume through the capsid pores, as a result of the entropic drive to maximize mixing, and a large osmotic pressure is developed inside the capsid to equalize the chemical potential of water inside and outside of the capsid.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic pressure

claim: Pressure inside the capsid can be described as DNA repulsion and bending pressure withstood by the capsid walls.
source: This pressure, due to the compressed water inside the rigid capsid volume can also be described as a DNA repulsion and bending pressure withstood by the capsid walls (Evilevitch et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evilevitch et al., 2008

claim: Addition of an osmolyte to the solution surrounding the capsid creates an osmotic gradient.
source: Addition of an osmolyte to the solution surrounding the capsid, where osmolyte is larger than the capsid pores, creates an osmotic gradient.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic pressure

claim: Water will be drawn out of the DNA volume to dilute the osmolyte molecules outside the capsid when osmolyte is added.
source: Water will be drawn out of the DNA volume to dilute the osmolyte molecules outside the capsid.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic pressure

claim: Addition of osmolyte reduces the water density and the osmotic pressure inside the capsid.
source: This reduces the water density and the osmotic pressure inside the capsid.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic pressure

claim: At critical osmolyte concentration c*, the pressure inside the capsid is brought down to one atmosphere.
source: Once the osmolyte concentration reaches c*, the pressure inside the capsid is brought down to one atm (atmospheric pressure).
evidence: Based on the mechanism of osmotic suppression

claim: At osmolyte concentration c*, the water-exchange equilibrium corresponds to zero osmotic pressure difference inside and outside the capsid.
source: For this special value of c*, the water-exchange equilibrium corresponds to zero osmotic pressure difference inside and outside the capsid and a net force of zero on the interior of the capsid's rigid walls conﬁning the DNA.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic equilibrium

claim: The osmotic pressure associated with the osmolyte concentration c* is equal to the osmotic pressure exerted by the confined DNA.
source: Thus, the osmotic pressure associated with the osmolyte concentration, c*, is equal to the osmotic pressure exerted by the conﬁned DNA.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic equilibrium

claim: At osmolyte concentration c*, DNA would not escape from the capsid even if allowed the opportunity because there is no driving force for this process.
source: As a consequence, even if the DNA was allowed the opportunity to ''escape'' from its conﬁnement (when the virus capsid is opened), it would not, because there is no driving force for this process.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic principles of osmotic equilibrium

claim: PEG 8 kDa was used to create osmotic pressure gradient because it does not permeate the capsid.
source: To create an osmotic pressure gradient between the interior and exterior of the capsid, we used PEG with molecular weight MW ≈ 8 kDa, which does not permeate the capsid since the HSV-1 capsid pore diameter is ~20 Å, corresponding to ~4 kDa MW cutoff (Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on capsid pore size measurements from Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003

claim: HSV-1 capsid pore diameter is approximately 20 Å, corresponding to approximately 4 kDa MW cutoff.
source: To create an osmotic pressure gradient between the interior and exterior of the capsid, we used PEG with molecular weight MW ≈ 8 kDa, which does not permeate the capsid since the HSV-1 capsid pore diameter is ~20 Å, corresponding to ~4 kDa MW cutoff (Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003

claim: DNA ejection from the capsid was triggered by mild trypsin treatment.
source: DNA ejection from the capsid was triggered by mild trypsin treatment.
evidence: Based on the experimental method described

claim: Trypsin cleaves the portal 'plug' proteins UL6 and UL25 while the rest of the HSV-1 capsid remains intact.
source: Trypsin cleaves the portal 'plug' proteins UL6 and UL25 while the rest of the HSV-1 capsid remains intact (Bauer et al., 2013; Newcomb et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bauer et al., 2013; Newcomb et al., 2007

claim: 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa corresponds to approximately 18 atm of external osmotic pressure equal to the DNA pressure in the HSV-1 capsid.
source: This corresponds to ~18 atm of external osmotic pressure equal to the DNA pressure in the capsid, at buffer conditions required for capsid binding to isolated nuclei, set by capsid binding buffer CBB (see Materials and methods Section).
evidence: Based on osmotic pressure calculations and experimental measurements

claim: Ionic conditions in the surrounding buffer affect DNA pressure in the capsid through cations permeating the capsid and screening the repulsive DNA-DNA interactions.
source: It should be noted that ionic conditions in the surrounding buffer also affect DNA pressure in the capsid through cations permeating the capsid and screening the repulsive DNA-DNA interactions (Evilevitch et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evilevitch et al., 2008

claim: Individual GFP-labeled HSV-1 C-capsids bind to NPCs on isolated DAPI-stained cell nuclei.
source: Figure 3 shows individual GFP-labeled HSV-1 C-capsids (green, strain K26GFP, HSV-1 strain expressing GFP-tagged VP26 protein) bound to NPCs on isolated DAPI-stained cell nuclei (blue), imaged with Super-Resolution Structured Illumination Microscopy (SR-SIM) (Sekine et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by SR-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3

claim: SR-SIM provides resolutions down to 120 nm, allowing visualization of individual capsids attached to the nucleus.
source: SR-SIM provides resolutions down to 120 nm, allowing visualization of individual capsids attached to the nucleus (HSV-1 C-capsid diameter ≈ 125 nm).
evidence: Based on the technical specifications of SR-SIM and capsid size

claim: HSV-1 C-capsid diameter is approximately 125 nm.
source: SR-SIM provides resolutions down to 120 nm, allowing visualization of individual capsids attached to the nucleus (HSV-1 C-capsid diameter ≈ 125 nm).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HSV-1 capsid structure

claim: Tegument-free C-capsids are able to bind efficiently to NPCs and eject DNA into a nucleus.
source: We found that tegument-free C-capsids were able to bind efficiently to NPCs and eject DNA into a nucleus.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in this study

claim: Untegumented C-capsids and viral capsids exposing inner tegument proteins on their surface have a similar degree of binding to NPCs.
source: This finding is consistent with a recent study demonstrating that untegumented C-capsids and viral capsids exposing inner tegument proteins on their surface had a similar degree of binding to NPCs (Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014

claim: DNA-filled C-capsids bind specifically to the NPCs as opposed to random binding to the nuclear membrane.
source: In parallel, using confocal fluorescent microscopy (FM), we confirmed that DNA-filled C-capsids bind specifically to the NPCs (as opposed to random binding to the nuclear membrane).
evidence: Supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data

claim: WGA (wheat germ agglutinin) blocks the NPC and prevents capsid binding.
source: As a control, we used WGA (wheat germ agglutinin) which blocks the NPC [WGA associates with the glycoproteins within the NPC (Ojala et al., 2000; Finlay et al., 1987) and competes with capsid binding], and prevents capsid binding, demonstrating capsid-NPC binding specificity, see Figure 3B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Finlay et al., 1987

claim: WGA associates with the glycoproteins within the NPC and competes with capsid binding.
source: As a control, we used WGA (wheat germ agglutinin) which blocks the NPC [WGA associates with the glycoproteins within the NPC (Ojala et al., 2000; Finlay et al., 1987) and competes with capsid binding], and prevents capsid binding, demonstrating capsid-NPC binding specificity, see Figure 3B.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Finlay et al., 1987

claim: Capsid-NPC binding is not inhibited by the addition of 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa.
source: Figure 3B also shows that capsid-NPC binding is not inhibited by the addition of 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa.
evidence: Supported by confocal fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 3B

claim: Nuclear transport through the NPCs is not negatively affected by hyperosmotic conditions corresponding to approximately 20 atm.
source: Finan et al. (2011) demonstrates that nuclear transport through the NPCs is not negatively affected by hyperosmotic conditions corresponding to those used in our study (~20 atm).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finan et al., 2011

claim: Under hyperosmotic stress, the nuclear size decreased while nuclear lacunarity increased, indicating expansion in the pores and channels interdigitating the chromatin.
source: Specifically, the authors reported that, under hyperosmotic stress, the nuclear size decreased while nuclear lacunarity increased, indicating expansion in the pores and channels interdigitating the chromatin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Finan et al., 2011

claim: The rate of nucleocytoplasmic transport increased under hyperosmotic stress due to the change in nucleus geometry, providing a shorter effective diffusion distance.
source: As a result, the rate of nucleocytoplasmic transport increased but only due to the change in nucleus geometry, providing a shorter effective diffusion distance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Finan et al., 2011

claim: Diffusivity within the nucleus was insensitive to the osmotic environment.
source: At the same time, the authors found that diffusivity within the nucleus was insensitive to the osmotic environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Finan et al., 2011

claim: Under hyperosmotic conditions at approximately 18 atm with 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa, the nuclei slightly shrunk.
source: In agreement with these studies (Finan et al., 2011), we observed that, under hyperosmotic conditions (~18 atm at 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa), the nuclei slightly shrunk (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The sub-nuclear structure of heterochromatin DNA was essentially unchanged upon addition of PEG.
source: However, the sub-nuclear structure of heterochromatin DNA was essentially unchanged upon addition of PEG, as visualized by a DAPI stain of nuclear DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, second row).
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The integrity of the nuclei was not affected by the addition of 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa as shown by fluorescently labeled 70 kDa dextran exclusion from the nuclei interior.
source: We also confirmed that the integrity of the nuclei was not affected by the addition of 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa by showing that fluorescently labeled 70 kDa dextran is excluded from the nuclei interior with nuclei remaining intact and structured, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: Supported by dextran exclusion assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The full transport functionality of NPCs is maintained in the reconstituted nuclei system at an osmotic pressure of approximately 18 atm generated by PEG.
source: Finally, we showed that the full transport functionality of NPCs is maintained in the reconstituted nuclei system at an osmotic pressure of ~18 atm generated by PEG.
evidence: Supported by NLS transport assay data

claim: GST-NLS-EGFP recombinant protein was fully transported into the nucleus through the NPC by an active mechanism at approximately 18 atm external osmotic pressure generated by PEG.
source: GST-NLS-EGFP was fully transported into the nucleus through the NPC by an active mechanism, which was detected by fluorescence microscopy (Miyamoto et al., 2002; Tsuji et al., 2007; Vázquez-Iglesias et al., 2009) (see details in the Materials and methods Section).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data and citations to Miyamoto et al., 2002; Tsuji et al., 2007; Vázquez-Iglesias et al., 2009

claim: The reconstituted capsid-nuclei system provides a robust assay for investigation of viral DNA ejection into a cell nucleus under hyperosmotic conditions.
source: Together, these findings show that the reconstituted capsid-nuclei system provides a robust assay for investigation of viral DNA ejection into a cell nucleus under hyperosmotic conditions.
evidence: Based on the validation experiments demonstrating nuclear integrity and NPC functionality

claim: After nuclei incubation with HSV-1 C-capsids at 37°C for 40 min without osmolyte addition, approximately 98% of all nuclei bound capsids ejected their DNA into nuclei.
source: After nuclei incubation with HSV-1 C-capsids at 37°C for 40 min without osmolyte addition, Figure 5D shows that ~98% of all nuclei bound capsids ejected their DNA into nuclei.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Viral DNA injection into nuclei did not affect the integrity of the nuclei.
source: Separately, using the fluorescently labeled 70 kDa dextran exclusion assay described in Section two above, we confirmed that viral DNA injection into nuclei did not affect the integrity of the nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by dextran exclusion assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 94–99% of the capsids in a given sample fraction are immunoprecipitated in the pull-down assay.
source: The efficiency of the pull-down assay was assessed by the DNase protection method where we showed that 94–99% of the capsids in a given sample fraction are immunoprecipitated (see method description and data in Materials and methods Section and table in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by DNase protection method data

claim: DNA copy numbers determined with the VP16 primer are generally higher than those determined with the ICP0 primer due to differences in qPCR amplification efficiency.
source: The fact that DNA copy numbers determined with the VP16 primer are generally higher than those determined with the ICP0 primer is related to the difference in qPCR amplification efficiency due to differences in primer-gene interactions.
evidence: Based on analysis of qPCR data and understanding of PCR amplification

claim: When the capsid pressure is turned off at 18 atm of external osmotic pressure, the ejection of DNA from capsids bound to nuclei is completely suppressed (fraction d/fractions c+d ~ 0.2%).
source: Figure 5B and D show that when the capsid pressure is turned off at 18 atm of external osmotic pressure, the ejection of DNA from capsids bound to nuclei is completely suppressed (fraction d/fractions c+d ~ 0.2%).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B and D

claim: DNA primers were selected to cover most of the HSV-1 genome length and included both S and L regions.
source: The positions of DNA primers were selected to cover most of the HSV-1 genome length and included both S and L regions corresponding to one copy of VP16 (103,163–104,635 bp) and the two copies of ICP0 [copy 1: (2,113 bp-5,388 bp) and copy 2: (120,207 bp-123,482 bp)].
evidence: Based on the experimental design for qPCR analysis

claim: DNA ejection from HSV-1 capsid follows directionality starting at the 151 kb S-end.
source: DNA ejection from HSV-1 capsid follows directionality starting at the 151 kb S-end (Newcomb et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Newcomb et al., 2009

claim: The primer selection ensured that both complete and partial ejection of the HSV-1 genome (151 kb total length) into the nucleus could be detected.
source: This primer selection ensured that both complete and partial ejection of the HSV-1 genome (151 kb total length) into the nucleus could be detected.
evidence: Based on the experimental design rationale

claim: The total DNA copy number added from all four fractions (a,b,c,d) separated with the pull-down assay remains the same with and without 30% w/w PEG added to the capsid-nuclei sample.
source: As a control, Figure 5C shows that the total DNA copy number added from all four fractions (a,b,c,d) separated with the pull-down assay remains the same with and without 30% w/w PEG added to the capsid-nuclei sample.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: No DNA is lost during the DNA fractionation steps due to PEG addition.
source: This confirms that no DNA is lost during the DNA fractionation steps due to PEG addition, and therefore the observed reduction in DNA amount in fraction d (ejected intranuclear DNA) is entirely attributed to the suppression of DNA ejection from nuclei-bound capsids.
evidence: Based on the control experiment showing total DNA remains constant

claim: The observed reduction in DNA amount in fraction d (ejected intranuclear DNA) is entirely attributed to the suppression of DNA ejection from nuclei-bound capsids.
source: This confirms that no DNA is lost during the DNA fractionation steps due to PEG addition, and therefore the observed reduction in DNA amount in fraction d (ejected intranuclear DNA) is entirely attributed to the suppression of DNA ejection from nuclei-bound capsids.
evidence: Based on the control experiment and experimental design

claim: The addition of 30% PEG 8 kDa does not interfere with capsid binding to nuclei.
source: As described above, fluorescent microscopy imaging in Figure 3B showed that the addition of 30% PEG 8 kDa does not interfere with capsid binding to nuclei.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 3B

claim: The number of capsids bound to nuclei is slightly increased with 30% PEG addition.
source: By determining the amounts of DNA injected into nuclei (fraction d) and retained in the capsids bound to nuclei (fraction c), Figure 5B shows that the number of capsids bound to nuclei is in fact slightly increased (fractions c and d combined) with 30% PEG addition (the number of unbound capsids in fraction b have correspondingly decreased).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Enhanced capsid binding to NPCs at nuclei can be explained by the crowding effect induced by PEG molecules.
source: Enhanced capsid binding to NPCs at nuclei can be explained by the crowding effect induced by PEG molecules, which has been observed to enhance macromolecular binding (Minton, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Minton, 2006 and inference from experimental observations

claim: Fraction a (free viral DNA in the extranuclear solution from broken capsids) is reduced by PEG addition.
source: Fraction a in Figure 5B, corresponding to free viral DNA in the extranuclear solution from broken capsids, is also reduced by PEG addition.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The reduction in fraction a is primarily attributed to the decreased number of unbound capsids in the extranuclear solution and also to increased capsid stability induced by PEG.
source: This is primarily attributed to the decreased number of unbound capsids in the extranuclear solution and also to increased capsid stability induced by PEG.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: Without PEG, fraction a only constitutes less than 0.2% of the total viral DNA amount and is at the level of qPCR background noise.
source: However, it should also be noted that even without PEG, fraction a only constitutes <0.2% of the total viral DNA amount and is at the level of qPCR background noise.
evidence: Based on qPCR data analysis

claim: Incubation of capsids with isolated nuclei with added cytosol at 4°C for 40 min without ATP regeneration system prevented DNA ejection from viral capsids with approximately 95% of HSV-1 capsids retaining their genomes.
source: As a negative control, capsids were first incubated with isolated nuclei with added cytosol at 4°C for 40 min without ATP regeneration system. As was previously observed (Ojala et al., 2000), these conditions prevented DNA ejection from viral capsids with ~95% of HSV-1 capsids retaining their genomes (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by EM data in Figure 6 and citation to Ojala et al., 2000

claim: After incubation of purified DNA-filled C-capsids with isolated rat liver nuclei in the presence of cell cytosol supplemented with ATP regeneration system for 40 min at 37°C, approximately 62% of capsids are empty with fully ejected DNA when no PEG is present.
source: After this incubation, Figure 6 shows EM micrographs of capsids attached to nuclei, where ~ 62% of capsids are empty with fully ejected DNA when no PEG is present (at least 100 nuclei bound capsids were counted for each sample analysis).
evidence: Supported by EM data in Figure 6

claim: The failure to eject DNA from the remaining approximately 38% of capsids can be attributed to the capsid damage and failure to attach to the NPCs.
source: The failure to eject DNA from the remaining ~38% of capsids can be attributed to the capsid damage and failure to attach to the NPCs.
evidence: Based on inference from EM observations

claim: Capsids bind to the nuclear membrane in multilayer clusters, where only the first layer, closest to the nuclear membrane, can dock to the NPCs and eject the DNA.
source: Indeed, Figure 6 shows capsids that bind to the nuclear membrane in multilayer clusters, where only the first layer, closest to the nuclear membrane, can dock to the NPCs and eject the DNA.
evidence: Supported by EM data in Figure 6

claim: When capsids were incubated with reconstituted nuclei for 40 min at 37°C with 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa present, the majority of capsids (approximately 81%) did not eject their genome and retained DNA in the capsid.
source: By contrast, Figure 6 shows that when capsids were incubated with reconstituted nuclei (in cytosol supplemented with ATP-regeneration system) for 40 min at 37°C with 30% w/w PEG 8 kDa present, the majority of capsids (~81%) did not eject their genome and retained DNA in the capsid.
evidence: Supported by EM data in Figure 6

claim: In the pull-down assay, the estimated fractions of capsids that ejected DNA without PEG or retained DNA with PEG present were even higher than in EM analysis.
source: In the pull-down assay, the estimated fractions of capsids that ejected DNA without PEG or retained DNA with PEG present, were even higher.
evidence: Based on comparison of pull-down assay and EM data

claim: In the pull-down assay, only capsids that were directly bound to nuclear NPCs were accounted for (fractions c and d), separated with several centrifugation steps and multiple washes of nuclei with bound capsids, unlike in the EM analysis where unbound capsids are also present.
source: This can be attributed to the fact that in the pull-down assay, only capsids that were directly bound to nuclear NPCs were accounted for (fractions c and d), separated with several centrifugation steps and multiple washes of nuclei with bound capsids, unlike in the EM analysis where unbound capsids are also present.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental methods

claim: The EM data qualitatively supports all of the pull-down assay observations.
source: Qualitatively, however, the EM data supports all of the pull-down assay observations above.
evidence: Based on comparison of EM and pull-down assay results

claim: NLS transport experiment and nucleocytoplasmic transport measurements under hyperosmotic stress showed that NPCs' transport functionality is not disrupted by 18 atm PEG-generated osmotic pressure.
source: The NLS transport experiment above (Section 2) and the nucleocytoplasmic transport measurements under hyperosmotic stress reported in Finan et al. (2011) showed that NPCs' transport functionality is not disrupted by 18 atm PEG-generated osmotic pressure.
evidence: Supported by NLS transport data and citation to Finan et al., 2011

claim: The observed suppression of DNA ejection from capsids into nuclei is caused by the osmotic pressure gradient across the capsid wall, which turns the capsid pressure off, as opposed to PEG itself and/or its osmotic pressure effect blocking the NPC channel.
source: Here, we further demonstrate that the observed suppression of DNA ejection from capsids into nuclei is caused by the osmotic pressure gradient across the capsid wall, which turns the capsid pressure off, as opposed to PEG itself and/or its osmotic pressure effect blocking the NPC channel and interfering with the transport functionality.
evidence: Supported by control experiments with PEG 400 Da

claim: At 17% w/w, PEG 400 generates 18 atm of osmotic pressure.
source: To show this, we repeated the capsid-nuclei binding experiment above but this time PEG 8 kDa was replaced with PEG 400 Da. At 17% w/w, PEG 400 generates 18 atm of osmotic pressure (see https://brocku.ca/researchers/peter_rand/).
evidence: Based on osmotic pressure calculations from reference source

claim: PEG 400 Da permeates the HSV-1 capsid.
source: However, as mentioned above, HSV-1 capsid pore size has a MW cutoff of ~4000 Da (Trus et al., 1996; Heymann et al., 2003); therefore, PEG 400 Da permeates the capsid (unlike PEG 8 kDa).
evidence: Based on capsid pore size and PEG molecular weight comparison

claim: When capsids bound to reconstituted nuclei are incubated at 18 atm osmotic pressure with PEG 400 Da, there will be no osmotic pressure gradient between inside and outside the capsid.
source: Accordingly, even when capsids bound to reconstituted nuclei are incubated at 18 atm osmotic pressure with PEG 400 Da, there will be no osmotic pressure gradient (between inside and outside the capsid) needed to cancel the DNA pressure in the capsid (Evilevitch et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on the mechanism of osmotic suppression and citation to Evilevitch et al., 2008

claim: When isolated nuclei reconstituted with cytosol and an ATP-regeneration system were incubated with C-capsids for 40 min at 37°C with 17% w/w PEG 400 Da added to the solution, approximately 60% of capsids were empty (ejected their DNA).
source: Indeed, when isolated nuclei reconstituted with cytosol and an ATP-regeneration system were incubated with C-capsids for 40 min at 37°C with 17% w/w PEG 400 Da added to the solution, ultrathin-sectioning EM (Figure 6) showed that, despite18 atm osmotic pressure surrounding the capsids,~60% of capsids were empty (ejected their DNA).
evidence: Supported by EM data in Figure 6

claim: The fraction of empty capsids that ejected DNA with 17% w/w PEG 400 Da (approximately 60%) is equivalent to the fraction of empty capsids that ejected DNA after incubation of capsids with reconstituted nuclei for 40 min at 37°C without PEG addition (approximately 62% empty capsids).
source: This is equivalent to the fraction of empty capsids that ejected DNA after incubation of capsids with reconstituted nuclei for 40 min at 37°C without PEG addition (~62% empty capsids).
evidence: Based on comparison of EM data with and without PEG 400 Da

claim: It is the osmotic pressure gradient that suppresses DNA ejection through the NPCs by 'turning off' the capsid pressure and not the interference with NPC transport functionality.
source: This observation further validates the assumption that it is the osmotic pressure gradient that suppresses DNA ejection through the NPCs by 'turning off' the capsid pressure and not the interference with NPC transport functionality.
evidence: Based on the control experiment with PEG 400 Da

claim: The pull-down assay and the EM data clearly demonstrate that viral DNA ejection into host nuclei from HSV-1 capsids bound to NPCs is completely blocked when the intracapsid genome pressure is turned off through an osmolyte addition.
source: Combined, the pull-down assay and the EM data clearly demonstrate that viral DNA ejection into host nuclei from HSV-1 capsids bound to NPCs is completely blocked when the intracapsid genome pressure is turned off through an osmolyte addition.
evidence: Supported by combined pull-down assay and EM data

claim: Viral DNA translocation from herpesvirus capsids across the nuclear membrane is driven by intracapsid pressure.
source: This proves that viral DNA translocation from herpesvirus capsids across the nuclear membrane is driven by intracapsid pressure.
evidence: Based on the experimental demonstration that DNA ejection is suppressed when capsid pressure is turned off

claim: All eukaryotic DNA viruses, with the exception of poxviruses, deliver and replicate their genomes within the nucleus.
source: All eukaryotic DNA viruses, with the exception of poxviruses, deliver and replicate their genomes within the nucleus (Hennig and O'Hare, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hennig and O'Hare, 2015

claim: Retroviruses transport their genomes across nuclear membranes in order to replicate after they have reversely transcribed their single-stranded RNA to dsDNA.
source: In addition, retro-viruses transport their genomes across nuclear membranes in order to replicate after they have reversely transcribed their single-stranded (ss) RNA to dsDNA.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of retrovirus replication

claim: The mechanism of viral DNA entry into the host nucleus remains poorly understood for the majority of viruses.
source: The mechanism of this most significant step of infection, viral DNA entry into the host nucleus, remains poorly understood for the majority of viruses (Hennig and O'Hare, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hennig and O'Hare, 2015

claim: The reconstituted capsid-nuclei experiments provide a demonstration of a nuclear entry mechanism of DNA from HSV-1, driven by high mechanical pressure of the encapsidated viral genome.
source: The reconstituted capsid-nuclei experiments above provide a demonstration of a nuclear entry mechanism of DNA from HSV-1, driven by high mechanical pressure of the encapsidated viral genome.
evidence: Based on the experimental findings in this study

claim: The role that capsid pressure plays for intranuclear viral genome delivery has not been demonstrated until now, despite previous measurements of intracapsid DNA pressure in several types of viruses.
source: Despite previous measurements of intracapsid DNA pressure in several types of viruses (Evilevitch et al., 2003; Bauer et al., 2013), the role that capsid pressure plays for intranuclear viral genome delivery has not been demonstrated until now.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Capsid pressure is critical for initiation of DNA ejection from a herpesvirus capsid into a host nucleus.
source: The aim of this work was to demonstrate that capsid pressure is critical for initiation of DNA ejection from a herpesvirus capsid into a host nucleus.
evidence: Based on the experimental findings in this study

claim: Other factors may contribute to complete internalization of the viral genome into the nucleus once the first portion of herpes DNA is released through the NPC channel by the capsid pressure.
source: However, other factors may contribute to complete internalization of the viral genome into the nucleus once the first portion of herpes DNA is released through the NPC channel by the capsid pressure.
evidence: Based on speculation about additional mechanisms

claim: Capsid pressure is rapidly reduced with the increasing fraction of ejected DNA.
source: As shown in Figure 2, capsid pressure is rapidly reduced with the increasing fraction of ejected DNA.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: At osmotic pressures of 3–4 atm, equivalent to that of the cellular cytoplasm surrounding the capsid, only approximately 50% of DNA is ejected.
source: At osmotic pressures of 3–4 atm, equivalent to that of the cellular cytoplasm surrounding the capsid (Jeembaeva et al., 2008), only ~50% of DNA is ejected.
evidence: Supported by data and citation to Jeembaeva et al., 2008

claim: Not all macromolecules generating the osmotic pressure in the cell are large enough not to penetrate the capsid.
source: However, not all macromolecules generating the osmotic pressure in the cell are large enough not to penetrate the capsid, which, as discussed above, is required for osmotic suppression of DNA ejection.
evidence: Based on inference about cellular osmotic environment

claim: The crowded cellular environment, combined with the presence of DNA-binding proteins in the cell, lead to instant condensation of the incoming viral DNA.
source: We had previously found that the crowded cellular environment (which contributes to the osmotic pressure [Parsegian et al., 2000]), combined with the presence of DNA-binding proteins in the cell, lead to instant condensation of the incoming viral DNA.
evidence: Supported by prior findings and citation to Parsegian et al., 2000

claim: DNA condensation exerts a significant pulling force on the rest of the DNA, facilitating its complete internalization in the cell.
source: This DNA condensation exerts a significant pulling force on the rest of the DNA, facilitating its complete internalization in the cell (Jeembaeva et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jeembaeva et al., 2008

claim: A recent theoretical study proposed that DNA ejection could be described by a two-step process, where the first portion of DNA is ejected by DNA-DNA repulsive pressure, followed by a slower process of anomalous diffusion of condensed viral genome in the crowded cytoplasm.
source: Further, a recent theoretical study proposed that DNA ejection could be described by a two-step process, where the first portion of DNA is ejected by DNA-DNA repulsive pressure, followed by a slower process of anomalous diffusion of condensed viral genome in the crowded cytoplasm (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018

claim: High intracapsid DNA packing density resulting in tens of atmospheres of pressure is a distinctive trait of all nine human herpesviruses.
source: High intracapsid DNA packing density resulting in tens of atmospheres of pressure is a distinctive trait of all nine human herpesviruses.
evidence: Based on calculations and structural data for herpesviruses

claim: Capsid DNA pressures in several types of herpesviruses were calculated using analytical expressions and EM measured values for inner capsid diameters.
source: In Figure 6—figure supplement 1, we calculated capsid DNA pressures in several types of herpesviruses using analytical expressions in refs. (Tzlil et al., 2003; Purohit et al., 2003) and EM measured values for inner capsid diameters (Booy et al., 1991; Germi et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017) to compute DNA-DNA electrostatic repulsive force and bending stress.
evidence: Supported by calculations based on cited theoretical models and structural data

claim: The calculated HSV-1 DNA pressure is in agreement with the measured value of 19 atm.
source: As a reference pressure, the calculated HSV-1 DNA pressure is in agreement with our measured value of 19 atm (Bauer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by comparison of calculated and measured values

claim: Computed pressures for different herpesviruses range from approximately 14 atm for VZV to approximately 90 atm for EBV.
source: The differences in computed pressures (ranging from ~14 atm for VZV to ~90 atm for EBV) are related to the variation in DNA packing density of these viruses (Booy et al., 1991; Germi et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by calculations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Differences in computed pressures for herpesviruses are related to the variation in DNA packing density of these viruses.
source: The differences in computed pressures (ranging from ~14 atm for VZV to ~90 atm for EBV) are related to the variation in DNA packing density of these viruses (Booy et al., 1991; Germi et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on calculations and structural data

claim: Pressure-driven entry of viral DNA into the host nucleus during infection is universal to all herpesviruses.
source: This strongly suggests that pressure-driven entry of viral DNA into the host nucleus during infection is universal to all herpesviruses.
evidence: Based on the finding that all herpesviruses have high DNA packing density and pressure

claim: Reoviruses replicate ssRNA to dsRNA inside the capsid during genome packaging, which results in genome packaging densities similar to that of herpesviruses.
source: For instance, during genome packaging, reoviruses replicate ssRNA to dsRNA inside the capsid, which results in genome packaging densities similar to that of herpesviruses (Prasad et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prasad et al., 1996

claim: Intracapsid replication in reoviruses could be regulated, at least in part, by generation of internal pressure resulting from the increasing genome packaging density as newly synthesized dsRNA continues to fill the internal capsid volume.
source: Such intracapsid replication could be regulated, at least in part, by generation of internal pressure resulting from the increasing genome packaging density as newly synthesized dsRNA continues to fill the internal capsid volume.
evidence: Based on speculation about pressure-regulated replication

claim: HIV capsids dock to NPCs at the nucleus and release transcribed dsDNA through the NPC channel.
source: Another example is HIV, where similar to herpesviruses, HIV capsids dock to NPCs at the nucleus and release transcribed dsDNA through the NPC channel (Rankovic et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rankovic et al., 2017

claim: The reverse transcription process from ssRNA to dsDNA inside the HIV capsid is associated with increasing internal DNA pressure.
source: It was recently shown that the reverse transcription process from ssRNA to dsDNA inside the HIV capsid is associated with increasing internal DNA pressure (Rankovic et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rankovic et al., 2017

claim: This work provides a platform for analysis of pressure-regulated replication in many viruses that afflict humans and animals.
source: By demonstrating the central function of herpes capsid pressure for intranuclear viral DNA entry, combined with assays developed in this work, we provide a platform for analysis of pressure-regulated replication in many viruses that afflict humans and animals.
evidence: Based on the implications of the experimental findings and methods developed

claim: Cytosol contains importin-β required for efficient HSV-1 capsid binding to NPCs.
source: Cytosol contains importin-β required for efficient HSV-1 capsid binding to NPCs (Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2014

claim: The ATP-regeneration system is not required for capsid binding to NPCs, but it is required for opening the capsid's portal leading to DNA ejection.
source: The ATP-regeneration system is not required for capsid binding to NPCs, but it is required for opening the capsid's portal leading to DNA ejection (Anderson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2014

claim: The ATP-regeneration system contains ATP and GTP, both of which are required for maintenance of the Ran-GTP/GDP gradient across the nuclear membrane.
source: The ATP-regeneration system contains ATP and GTP (as well as other components [Ojala et al., 2000]), both of which are required for maintenance of the Ran-GTP/GDP gradient across the nuclear membrane (Cole and Hammell, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ojala et al., 2000; Cole and Hammell, 1998

claim: Importin-β binds to cargo proteins.
source: While the mechanisms of interactions that mediate capsid docking to NPC and its opening are not clear, importin-β binds to cargo proteins (Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001), while the Ran-GTP cycle regulates the importin-cargo association (Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001

claim: The Ran-GTP cycle regulates the importin-cargo association.
source: While the mechanisms of interactions that mediate capsid docking to NPC and its opening are not clear, importin-β binds to cargo proteins (Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001), while the Ran-GTP cycle regulates the importin-cargo association (Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cautain et al., 2015; Macara, 2001

claim: A nuclear localization signal (NLS) and other motifs on viral capsid proteins are involved in importin binding interaction.
source: A nuclear localization signal (NLS) and other motifs on viral capsid proteins are involved in this importin binding interaction (Cole and Hammell, 1998; Flatt and Greber, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cole and Hammell, 1998; Flatt and Greber, 2015

claim: Herpes DNA does not interact with import protein factors.
source: Since herpes DNA does not interact with import protein factors, these protein factors are likely involved in the binding and opening of the capsid portal vertex, which triggers genome ejection, but they do not provide the driving force for the actual translocation of the viral DNA across the NPC channel (which is driven by DNA capsid pressure, as we demonstrate below).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings

claim: Import protein factors are likely involved in the binding and opening of the capsid portal vertex, which triggers genome ejection, but they do not provide the driving force for the actual translocation of the viral DNA across the NPC channel.
source: Since herpes DNA does not interact with import protein factors, these protein factors are likely involved in the binding and opening of the capsid portal vertex, which triggers genome ejection, but they do not provide the driving force for the actual translocation of the viral DNA across the NPC channel (which is driven by DNA capsid pressure, as we demonstrate below).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings
